claim: Abnormal expansions of GGGGCC repeat sequence in the noncoding region of the C9orf72 gene is the most common cause of familial amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and frontotemporal dementia (C9-ALS/FTD).
source: Abnormal expansions of GGGGCC repeat sequence in the noncoding region of the C9orf72 gene is the most common cause of familial amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and frontotemporal dementia (C9-ALS/FTD).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature in the field.

claim: The expanded repeat sequence is translated into dipeptide repeat proteins (DPRs) by noncanonical repeat-associated non-AUG (RAN) translation.
source: The expanded repeat sequence is translated into dipeptide repeat proteins (DPRs) by noncanonical repeat-associated non-AUG (RAN) translation.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations.

claim: DPRs play central roles in the pathogenesis of C9-ALS/FTD.
source: Since DPRs play central roles in the pathogenesis of C9-ALS/FTD, we here investigate the regulatory mechanisms of RAN translation, focusing on the effects of RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) targeting GGGGCC repeat RNAs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and serves as the rationale for the current study.

claim: The ALS/FTD-linked RBP FUS suppresses RAN translation and neurodegeneration in C9-ALS/FTD model flies in an RNA-binding activity-dependent manner.
source: Using C9-ALS/FTD model flies, we demonstrated that the ALS/FTD-linked RBP FUS suppresses RAN translation and neurodegeneration in an RNA-binding activity-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Drosophila models presented in the manuscript.

claim: FUS directly binds to and modulates the G-quadruplex structure of GGGGCC repeat RNA as an RNA chaperone.
source: Moreover, we found that FUS directly binds to and modulates the G-quadruplex structure of GGGGCC repeat RNA as an RNA chaperone, resulting in the suppression of RAN translation in vitro.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro experimental data including CD spectroscopy, NMR, and binding assays.

claim: FUS modulation of G-quadruplex structure results in the suppression of RAN translation in vitro.
source: Moreover, we found that FUS directly binds to and modulates the G-quadruplex structure of GGGGCC repeat RNA as an RNA chaperone, resulting in the suppression of RAN translation in vitro.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro translation assay data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Abnormal expansions of the GGGGCC (G4C2) repeat sequence in the noncoding region of the C9orf72 gene have been found to be the most common genetic mutation responsible for ALS/FTD.
source: Abnormal expansions of the GGGGCC (G4C2) repeat sequence in the noncoding region of the C9orf72 gene have been found to be the most common genetic mutation responsible for ALS/FTD (DeJesus-Hernandez et al., 2011; Gijselinck et al., 2012; Renton et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three key papers that discovered this mutation.

claim: Expansion of the G4C2 repeats results in decreased expression of the C9orf72 gene, leading to its haploinsufficiency.
source: first, expansion of the G4C2 repeats results in decreased expression of the C9orf72 gene, leading to its haploinsufficiency (Boivin et al., 2020; DeJesus-Hernandez et al., 2011; Gijselinck et al., 2012; Shi et al., 2018; Waite et al., 2014; Zhu et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The transcribed G4C2 repeat-containing RNA accumulates as RNA foci in the affected tissues, sequestering various RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) and altering their function.
source: Second, the transcribed G4C2 repeat-containing RNA accumulates as RNA foci in the affected tissues, sequestering various RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) and altering their function (Conlon et al., 2016; Cooper-Knock et al., 2014; Donnelly et al., 2013; Haeusler et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2013; Mori et al., 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: G4C2 repeat RNA is translated into dipeptide repeat (DPR) proteins, despite the lack of an AUG initiation codon, by noncanonical repeat-associated non-AUG (RAN) translation.
source: Third, this G4C2 repeat RNA is also translated into dipeptide repeat (DPR) proteins, despite the lack of an AUG initiation codon, by noncanonical repeat-associated non-AUG (RAN) translation (Ash et al., 2013; Gendron et al., 2013; Mori et al., 2013b; Mori et al., 2013c; Zu et al., 2011; Zu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: RAN translation occurs in all reading frames and the expanded G4C2 repeat sequence is bidirectionally transcribed.
source: Since RAN translation occurs in all reading frames and the expanded G4C2 repeat sequence is bidirectionally transcribed, five distinct DPRs, that is, poly(glycine-arginine) [poly(GR)], poly(glycine-alanine) [poly(GA)], poly(glycine-proline) [poly(GP)], poly(proline-arginine) [poly(PR)], and poly(proline-alanine) [poly(PA)], are produced and observed in patients' brains (Ash et al., 2013; Gendron et al., 2013; Mori et al., 2013b; Mori et al., 2013c; Zu et al., 2013) and cerebrospinal fluid (Gendron et al., 2017; Krishnan et al., 2022; Lehmer et al., 2017; Su et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Five distinct DPRs are produced: poly(GR), poly(GA), poly(GP), poly(PR), and poly(PA).
source: Since RAN translation occurs in all reading frames and the expanded G4C2 repeat sequence is bidirectionally transcribed, five distinct DPRs, that is, poly(glycine-arginine) [poly(GR)], poly(glycine-alanine) [poly(GA)], poly(glycine-proline) [poly(GP)], poly(proline-arginine) [poly(PR)], and poly(proline-alanine) [poly(PA)], are produced and observed in patients' brains (Ash et al., 2013; Gendron et al., 2013; Mori et al., 2013b; Mori et al., 2013c; Zu et al., 2013) and cerebrospinal fluid (Gendron et al., 2017; Krishnan et al., 2022; Lehmer et al., 2017; Su et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: DPRs are observed in patients' brains and cerebrospinal fluid.
source: Since RAN translation occurs in all reading frames and the expanded G4C2 repeat sequence is bidirectionally transcribed, five distinct DPRs, that is, poly(glycine-arginine) [poly(GR)], poly(glycine-alanine) [poly(GA)], poly(glycine-proline) [poly(GP)], poly(proline-arginine) [poly(PR)], and poly(proline-alanine) [poly(PA)], are produced and observed in patients' brains (Ash et al., 2013; Gendron et al., 2013; Mori et al., 2013b; Mori et al., 2013c; Zu et al., 2013) and cerebrospinal fluid (Gendron et al., 2017; Krishnan et al., 2022; Lehmer et al., 2017; Su et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: DPRs have been shown to exert toxic effects in multiple C9-ALS/FTD models, such as cultured cells, flies, and mice.
source: DPRs have been shown to exert toxic effects in multiple C9-ALS/FTD models, such as cultured cells, flies, and mice (Choi et al., 2019; Jovičić et al., 2015; May et al., 2014; Mizielinska et al., 2014; Rudich et al., 2017; Wen et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: DPR-only flies, which express DPRs translated from non-G4C2 repeat RNAs with alternative codons, show neurodegeneration.
source: Importantly, the toxicity of DPRs was confirmed in DPR-only flies, which express DPRs translated from non-G4C2 repeat RNAs with alternative codons and show neurodegeneration, whereas RNA-only flies expressing G4C2 repeat RNAs with stop codon interruptions, which eliminate DPRs production, did not show any obvious degenerative phenotypes (Mizielinska et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: RNA-only flies expressing G4C2 repeat RNAs with stop codon interruptions, which eliminate DPRs production, did not show any obvious degenerative phenotypes.
source: Importantly, the toxicity of DPRs was confirmed in DPR-only flies, which express DPRs translated from non-G4C2 repeat RNAs with alternative codons and show neurodegeneration, whereas RNA-only flies expressing G4C2 repeat RNAs with stop codon interruptions, which eliminate DPRs production, did not show any obvious degenerative phenotypes (Mizielinska et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Increased DPR production, but not RNA foci, was reported to correlate with G4C2 repeat-induced toxicity in a C9-ALS/FTD Drosophila model.
source: In addition, increased DPR production, but not RNA foci, was reported to correlate with G4C2 repeat-induced toxicity in a C9-ALS/FTD Drosophila model (Tran et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: DPRs have been reported to disrupt various biological pathways, such as nucleocytoplasmic transport and membraneless organelle dynamics.
source: Indeed, DPRs have been reported to disrupt various biological pathways, such as nucleocytoplasmic transport (Hutten et al., 2020; Jovičić et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2016) and membraneless organelle dynamics (Kwon et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2016; Lin et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Previous studies on C9-ALS/FTD using monocistronic reporters containing a G4C2 repeat sequence revealed cap-dependent translation initiation from the upstream near-cognate CUG initiation codon, requiring the cap-binding eukaryotic translation factor 4F complex.
source: Previous studies on C9-ALS/FTD using monocistronic reporters containing a G4C2 repeat sequence revealed cap-dependent translation initiation from the upstream near-cognate CUG initiation codon, requiring the cap-binding eukaryotic translation factor 4F complex (Green et al., 2017; Tabet et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Studies using bicistronic reporters with a G4C2 repeat sequence in the second cistron produced DPRs by RAN translation in all reading frames, suggesting cap-independent translation initiation within the G4C2 repeat sequence.
source: On the other hand, studies using bicistronic reporters with a G4C2 repeat sequence in the second cistron also produced DPRs by RAN translation in all reading frames, suggesting cap-independent translation initiation within the G4C2 repeat sequence (Cheng et al., 2018; Sonobe et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: RAN translation shows repeat length dependency.
source: Considering a repeat length dependency of RAN translation (Mori et al., 2013c; Zu et al., 2011; Zu et al., 2013), the repeat sequence itself would also be essential for the initiation or elongation steps of RAN translation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The repeat sequence itself is essential for the initiation or elongation steps of RAN translation.
source: Considering a repeat length dependency of RAN translation (Mori et al., 2013c; Zu et al., 2011; Zu et al., 2013), the repeat sequence itself would also be essential for the initiation or elongation steps of RAN translation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the repeat length dependency of RAN translation.

claim: TDP-43 plays a protective role on UGGAA repeat-induced toxicity in spinocerebellar ataxia type 31 (SCA31) models.
source: Based on our previous findings of the protective role of TDP-43 on UGGAA repeat-induced toxicity in spinocerebellar ataxia type 31 (SCA31) models (Ishiguro et al., 2017), we hypothesized that RBPs specifically binding to repeat sequences of template RNA play a role in RAN translation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: Coexpression of FUS, IGF2BP1, or hnRNPA2B1 strongly suppressed the eye degeneration in both flies expressing (G4C2)42 or 89.
source: We found that coexpression of FUS, IGF2BP1, or hnRNPA2B1 strongly suppressed the eye degeneration in both flies expressing (G4C2)42 or 89, which show decreased eye size and loss of pigmentation (Figure 1A–D and Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Flies expressing (G4C2)42 or 89 show decreased eye size and loss of pigmentation.
source: We found that coexpression of FUS, IGF2BP1, or hnRNPA2B1 strongly suppressed the eye degeneration in both flies expressing (G4C2)42 or 89, which show decreased eye size and loss of pigmentation (Figure 1A–D and Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Coexpression of hnRNPR, SAFB2, SF3B3, hnRNPA1, and hnRNPL partially suppressed the eye degeneration.
source: Coexpression of five RBPs, namely, hnRNPR, SAFB2, SF3B3, hnRNPA1, and hnRNPL, also partially suppressed the eye degeneration, whereas coexpression of the other six RBPs had no effect, and two RBPs enhanced the phenotypes (Figure 1A–D and Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Coexpression of six RBPs had no effect on eye degeneration, and two RBPs enhanced the phenotypes.
source: Coexpression of five RBPs, namely, hnRNPR, SAFB2, SF3B3, hnRNPA1, and hnRNPL, also partially suppressed the eye degeneration, whereas coexpression of the other six RBPs had no effect, and two RBPs enhanced the phenotypes (Figure 1A–D and Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Coexpression of TDP-43 had no effect on the eye degeneration in (G4C2)42 flies and resulted in lethality in (G4C2)89 flies.
source: In addition, coexpression of TDP-43 had no effect on the eye degeneration in (G4C2)42 flies and resulted in lethality in (G4C2)89 flies, likely due to the toxicity of TDP-43 expression itself (Figure 1A and D and Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The lethality in (G4C2)89 flies coexpressing TDP-43 is likely due to the toxicity of TDP-43 expression itself.
source: In addition, coexpression of TDP-43 had no effect on the eye degeneration in (G4C2)42 flies and resulted in lethality in (G4C2)89 flies, likely due to the toxicity of TDP-43 expression itself (Figure 1A and D and Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning based on the observed lethality.

claim: Coexpression of IGF2BP1 or hnRNPA2B1 significantly decreased G4C2 repeat RNA levels.
source: We found that coexpression of IGF2BP1 or hnRNPA2B1 significantly decreased G4C2 repeat RNA levels, whereas they were not altered upon coexpression of FUS (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: G4C2 repeat RNA levels were not altered upon coexpression of FUS.
source: We found that coexpression of IGF2BP1 or hnRNPA2B1 significantly decreased G4C2 repeat RNA levels, whereas they were not altered upon coexpression of FUS (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The suppressive effects of IGF2BP1 and hnRNPA2B1 could be explained by the decreased levels of G4C2 repeat RNA.
source: Although the suppressive effects of IGF2BP1 and hnRNPA2B1 could simply be explained by the decreased levels of G4C2 repeat RNA, the molecular mechanisms by which FUS suppresses G4C2 repeat-induced toxicity remain to be clarified.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observed correlation between decreased RNA levels and suppression of toxicity.

claim: The molecular mechanisms by which FUS suppresses G4C2 repeat-induced toxicity remain to be clarified.
source: Although the suppressive effects of IGF2BP1 and hnRNPA2B1 could simply be explained by the decreased levels of G4C2 repeat RNA, the molecular mechanisms by which FUS suppresses G4C2 repeat-induced toxicity remain to be clarified.
evidence: This statement acknowledges a gap in understanding that the study aims to address.

claim: Coexpression of FUS using multiple FUS fly lines significantly suppressed decreased eye size and loss of pigmentation in (G4C2)42 or 89 flies.
source: The suppressive effects of FUS on G4C2 repeat-induced toxicity were confirmed using multiple FUS fly lines, showing the significant suppression of decreased eye size and loss of pigmentation in (G4C2)42 or 89 flies coexpressing FUS (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: His-tagged FUS binds to the (G4C2)4 RNA in a dose-dependent manner.
source: We found that His-tagged FUS binds to the (G4C2)4 RNA in a dose-dependent manner, but not to the control (AAAAAA)4 RNA (Figure 5A), and His-tagged FUS-RRMmut had almost no binding affinity to the (G4C2)4 RNA, consistent with a previous study (Mori et al., 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from filter binding assay shown in Figure 5A.

claim: His-tagged FUS does not bind to the control (AAAAAA)4 RNA.
source: We found that His-tagged FUS binds to the (G4C2)4 RNA in a dose-dependent manner, but not to the control (AAAAAA)4 RNA (Figure 5A), and His-tagged FUS-RRMmut had almost no binding affinity to the (G4C2)4 RNA, consistent with a previous study (Mori et al., 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from filter binding assay shown in Figure 5A.

claim: His-tagged FUS-RRMmut had almost no binding affinity to the (G4C2)4 RNA.
source: We found that His-tagged FUS binds to the (G4C2)4 RNA in a dose-dependent manner, but not to the control (AAAAAA)4 RNA (Figure 5A), and His-tagged FUS-RRMmut had almost no binding affinity to the (G4C2)4 RNA, consistent with a previous study (Mori et al., 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from filter binding assay shown in Figure 5A and is consistent with prior research.

claim: FUS colocalizes with RNA foci in C9-ALS/FTD flies.
source: We also confirmed the interaction of FUS with the G4C2 repeat RNA in our C9-ALS/FTD flies by showing the colocalization of FUS with the RNA foci (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), consistent with a recent study using C9-ALS/FTD patient fibroblasts (Bajc Česnik et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: G4C2 repeat RNA forms both G-quadruplex and hairpin structures.
source: Since G4C2 repeat RNA was reported to form both G-quadruplex and hairpin structures (Fratta et al., 2012; Haeusler et al., 2014; Reddy et al., 2013; Su et al., 2014), we next characterized the interactions of FUS with G4C2 repeat RNA having different structures.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: G4C2 repeat RNA forms G-quadruplex structures in the presence of K+.
source: G4C2 repeat RNA is known to form G-quadruplex structures in the presence of K+, whereas they form hairpin structures in the presence of Na+ (Su et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: G4C2 repeat RNA forms hairpin structures in the presence of Na+.
source: G4C2 repeat RNA is known to form G-quadruplex structures in the presence of K+, whereas they form hairpin structures in the presence of Na+ (Su et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: FUS preferentially binds to (G4C2)4 RNA with the G-quadruplex structure in KCl buffer (KD = 1.5 × 10–8 M).
source: Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) analyses demonstrated that FUS preferentially binds to (G4C2)4 RNA with the G-quadruplex structure in KCl buffer (Table 1, dissociation constant (KD) = 1.5 × 10–8 M) and weakly to (G4C2)4 RNA with the hairpin structure in NaCl buffer (Table 1, KD = 1.3 × 10–7 μM).
evidence: This claim is supported by SPR data shown in Table 1.

claim: FUS weakly binds to (G4C2)4 RNA with the hairpin structure in NaCl buffer (KD = 1.3 × 10–7 μM).
source: Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) analyses demonstrated that FUS preferentially binds to (G4C2)4 RNA with the G-quadruplex structure in KCl buffer (Table 1, dissociation constant (KD) = 1.5 × 10–8 M) and weakly to (G4C2)4 RNA with the hairpin structure in NaCl buffer (Table 1, KD = 1.3 × 10–7 μM).
evidence: This claim is supported by SPR data shown in Table 1.

claim: FUS has poor binding affinity to (G4C2)4 RNA in LiCl buffer (KD = 1.4 × 10–5 μM).
source: We also confirmed that FUS has poor binding affinity to (G4C2)4 RNA in LiCl buffer (Table 1, KD = 1.4 × 10–5 μM), which destabilizes the G-quadruplex structure (Hardin et al., 1992), and was an almost similar level to its binding affinity to the negative control (A4C2)4 RNA (not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by SPR data shown in Table 1.

claim: LiCl destabilizes the G-quadruplex structure.
source: We also confirmed that FUS has poor binding affinity to (G4C2)4 RNA in LiCl buffer (Table 1, KD = 1.4 × 10–5 μM), which destabilizes the G-quadruplex structure (Hardin et al., 1992), and was an almost similar level to its binding affinity to the negative control (A4C2)4 RNA (not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: FUS preferentially binds to G-quadruplex structured Sc1 and DNMT RNAs.
source: These results suggest the preferential binding of FUS to G4C2 repeat RNA with the G-quadruplex structure, which is consistent with a previous report showing preferential binding of FUS to G-quadruplex structured Sc1 and DNMT RNAs (Ozdilek et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Higher-order structures, including G-quadruplex and hairpin structures, are involved in RAN translation.
source: Considering that higher-order structures, including G-quadruplex and hairpin structures, are reported to be involved in RAN translation (Mori et al., 2021; Simone et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2019; Zu et al., 2011), we next investigated the effects of FUS on the structure of G4C2 repeat RNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The CD spectrum of (G4C2)4 RNA in KCl buffer exhibits a positive peak at approximately 260 nm and a negative peak at 240 nm.
source: The circular dichroism (CD) spectrum of (G4C2)4 RNA in KCl buffer was found to exhibit a positive peak at approximately 260 nm and a negative peak at 240 nm (Figure 5B, black line), consistent with previous reports (Fratta et al., 2012; Haeusler et al., 2014; Reddy et al., 2013; Su et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by CD spectroscopy data shown in Figure 5B and is consistent with prior research.

claim: Upon the addition of FUS, the two peaks in the CD spectrum of (G4C2)4 RNA were notably shifted to longer wavelengths with substantial CD spectrum changes.
source: Interestingly, upon the addition of FUS, these two peaks were notably shifted to longer wavelengths with substantial CD spectrum changes, indicating a significant structural alteration in (G4C2)4 RNA (Figure 5B, red line).
evidence: This claim is supported by CD spectroscopy data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The addition of FUS causes a significant structural alteration in (G4C2)4 RNA.
source: Interestingly, upon the addition of FUS, these two peaks were notably shifted to longer wavelengths with substantial CD spectrum changes, indicating a significant structural alteration in (G4C2)4 RNA (Figure 5B, red line).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the CD spectroscopy data showing spectral changes.

claim: The CD spectrum of FUS alone in the wavelength range of 240–300 nm is almost negligible.
source: We confirmed that the CD spectrum of FUS alone in the wavelength range of 240–300 nm was almost negligible (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, green line), indicating that this change in CD spectrum is attributed to structural changes in the (G4C2)4 RNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by CD spectroscopy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The change in CD spectrum upon FUS addition is attributed to structural changes in the (G4C2)4 RNA.
source: We confirmed that the CD spectrum of FUS alone in the wavelength range of 240–300 nm was almost negligible (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, green line), indicating that this change in CD spectrum is attributed to structural changes in the (G4C2)4 RNA.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the negligible CD signal of FUS alone.

claim: CD spectrum changes were observed to some extent in the (G4C2)4 RNA upon the addition of FUS in NaCl buffer.
source: We also observed CD spectrum changes to some extent in the (G4C2)4 RNA upon the addition of FUS in NaCl buffer, but not in LiCl buffer, confirming an interaction between FUS and hairpin-structured (G4C2)4 RNA as well (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by CD spectroscopy data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: No CD spectrum changes were observed in the (G4C2)4 RNA upon the addition of FUS in LiCl buffer.
source: We also observed CD spectrum changes to some extent in the (G4C2)4 RNA upon the addition of FUS in NaCl buffer, but not in LiCl buffer, confirming an interaction between FUS and hairpin-structured (G4C2)4 RNA as well (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by CD spectroscopy data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: FUS interacts with hairpin-structured (G4C2)4 RNA.
source: We also observed CD spectrum changes to some extent in the (G4C2)4 RNA upon the addition of FUS in NaCl buffer, but not in LiCl buffer, confirming an interaction between FUS and hairpin-structured (G4C2)4 RNA as well (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the CD spectroscopy data showing changes in NaCl buffer.

claim: NMR signals of the imino proton for the G-quadruplex structure of (G4C2)4 RNA were detected in the region around 10–12 ppm in KCl buffer.
source: In KCl buffer, the NMR signals of the imino proton for the G-quadruplex structure of (G4C2)4 RNA were detected in the region around 10–12 ppm (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D), consistent with previous studies (Fratta et al., 2012; Su et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D and is consistent with prior research.

claim: Upon the addition of FUS, the NMR intensities of (G4C2)4 RNA decreased in an FUS concentration-dependent manner.
source: Upon the addition of FUS, the NMR intensities of (G4C2)4 RNA were decreased in an FUS concentration-dependent manner (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D), further supporting the possibility that that FUS interacts with and modulates the G-quadruplex structure of (G4C2)4 RNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D.

claim: FUS interacts with and modulates the G-quadruplex structure of (G4C2)4 RNA.
source: Upon the addition of FUS, the NMR intensities of (G4C2)4 RNA were decreased in an FUS concentration-dependent manner (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D), further supporting the possibility that that FUS interacts with and modulates the G-quadruplex structure of (G4C2)4 RNA.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the NMR data showing concentration-dependent changes.

claim: FUS directly binds to G4C2 repeat RNA, preferentially to its G-quadruplex form and modulates its higher-order structures.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that FUS directly binds to G4C2 repeat RNA, preferentially to its G-quadruplex form and modulates its higher-order structures.
evidence: This claim is a synthesis of multiple experimental findings including SPR, CD, and NMR data.

claim: Structural alterations of G4C2 repeat RNAs by FUS did not require ATP or interactions with other proteins.
source: These structural alterations of G4C2 repeat RNAs by FUS did not require ATP or interactions with other proteins, suggesting its role as an RNA chaperone for G4C2 repeat RNA (Rajkowitsch et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is based on the experimental conditions used and is supported by citation to the definition of RNA chaperones.

claim: FUS functions as an RNA chaperone for G4C2 repeat RNA.
source: These structural alterations of G4C2 repeat RNAs by FUS did not require ATP or interactions with other proteins, suggesting its role as an RNA chaperone for G4C2 repeat RNA (Rajkowitsch et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the ATP-independent structural modulation and is supported by citation to RNA chaperone definition.

claim: The reporter system produces GA-Myc by RAN translation.
source: We confirmed by western blotting that this reporter system indeed produces GA-Myc by RAN translation, consistent with previous studies (Green et al., 2017; Tabet et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data and is consistent with prior research.

claim: FUS suppressed RAN translation efficiently in the in vitro translation system.
source: Notably, upon the addition to this translation system, FUS suppressed RAN translation efficiently, whereas FUS-RRMmut did not.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro translation assay data.

claim: FUS-RRMmut did not suppress RAN translation efficiently in the in vitro translation system.
source: Notably, upon the addition to this translation system, FUS suppressed RAN translation efficiently, whereas FUS-RRMmut did not.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro translation assay data.

claim: FUS decreased the expression levels of GA-Myc at as low as 10 nM and nearly eliminated RAN translation activity at 100 nM.
source: FUS decreased the expression levels of GA-Myc at as low as 10 nM and nearly eliminated RAN translation activity at 100 nM.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro translation assay data.

claim: At 400 nM, FUS-RRMmut weakly suppressed the GA-Myc expression levels probably because of the residual RNA-binding activity.
source: At 400 nM, FUS-RRMmut weakly suppressed the GA-Myc expression levels probably because of the residual RNA-binding activity (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro translation assay data and includes speculative reasoning about residual activity.

claim: FUS suppresses RAN translation in vitro through direct interactions with G4C2 repeat RNA as an RNA chaperone.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that FUS suppresses RAN translation in vitro through direct interactions with G4C2 repeat RNA as an RNA chaperone.
evidence: This claim is a synthesis of multiple experimental findings including binding assays, structural analyses, and in vitro translation assays.

claim: Coexpression of EWSR1, DDX3X, DDX5, or DDX17 significantly suppressed eye degeneration in (G4C2)89 flies without altering G4C2 RNA expression.
source: Intriguingly, coexpression of EWSR1, DDX3X, DDX5, or DDX17 significantly suppressed eye degeneration in (G4C2)89 flies without altering G4C2 RNA expression (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: EWSR1, DDX3X, DDX5, and DDX17 decreased the number of poly(GA) aggregates in the eye imaginal discs.
source: As expected, these RBPs also decreased the number of poly(GA) aggregates in the eye imaginal discs (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6E and F.

claim: Coexpression of DHX9 or DHX36 suppressed eye degeneration by reducing G4C2 repeat RNA levels.
source: On the other hand, coexpression of DHX9 or DHX36 suppressed eye degeneration by reducing G4C2 repeat RNA levels (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: DDX3X was previously reported to suppress RAN translation and G4C2 repeat-induced toxicity in cell culture in a helicase-activity-dependent manner.
source: In support of our results, DDX3X was previously reported to suppress RAN translation and G4C2 repeat-induced toxicity in cell culture in a helicase-activity-dependent manner (Cheng et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: G-quadruplex-targeting RBPs have diverse biological functions, including transcription, RNA processing, translation, and RNA stabilization.
source: Since G-quadruplex-targeting RBPs have diverse biological functions, including transcription, RNA processing, translation, and RNA stabilization (Dumas et al., 2021), these different effects among G-quadruplex-targeting RBPs on G4C2 repeat RNA expression might be attributed to their different roles in RNA metabolism.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Different effects among G-quadruplex-targeting RBPs on G4C2 repeat RNA expression might be attributed to their different roles in RNA metabolism.
source: Since G-quadruplex-targeting RBPs have diverse biological functions, including transcription, RNA processing, translation, and RNA stabilization (Dumas et al., 2021), these different effects among G-quadruplex-targeting RBPs on G4C2 repeat RNA expression might be attributed to their different roles in RNA metabolism.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning based on known functions of RBPs.

claim: Some G-quadruplex-targeting RBPs regulate RAN translation and G4C2 repeat-induced toxicity by binding to and possibly by modulating the G-quadruplex structure of G4C2 repeat RNA.
source: Thus, some G-quadruplex-targeting RBPs regulate RAN translation and G4C2 repeat-induced toxicity by binding to and possibly by modulating the G-quadruplex structure of G4C2 repeat RNA.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data on multiple G-quadruplex-targeting RBPs.

claim: Coexpression of FUS-RRMmut did not restore the eye degeneration in flies expressing (G4C2)89.
source: We found that coexpression of FUS-RRMmut did not restore the eye degeneration in flies expressing (G4C2)89, suggesting that the RNA-binding activity of FUS is essential for its suppressive effects on G4C2 repeat-induced toxicity (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The RNA-binding activity of FUS is essential for its suppressive effects on G4C2 repeat-induced toxicity.
source: We found that coexpression of FUS-RRMmut did not restore the eye degeneration in flies expressing (G4C2)89, suggesting that the RNA-binding activity of FUS is essential for its suppressive effects on G4C2 repeat-induced toxicity (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of suppression by FUS-RRMmut.

claim: The reduced egg-to-adult viability of (G4C2)42 flies was rescued by coexpression of FUS, but not by coexpression of FUS-RRMmut.
source: We also evaluated the reduced egg-to-adult viability of (G4C2)42 flies and confirmed that this phenotype was rescued by coexpression of FUS, but not by coexpression of FUS-RRMmut (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Coexpression of FUS significantly alleviated motor dysfunction in flies expressing G4C2 repeat RNA in the nervous system.
source: Expression of G4C2 repeat RNA in the nervous system of flies after eclosion using the elav-GeneSwitch driver induces motor dysfunction, and coexpression of FUS significantly alleviated this motor dysfunction (Figure 2E), indicating that FUS suppresses the neuronal phenotypes of flies expressing G4C2 repeat RNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: FUS suppresses the neuronal phenotypes of flies expressing G4C2 repeat RNA.
source: Expression of G4C2 repeat RNA in the nervous system of flies after eclosion using the elav-GeneSwitch driver induces motor dysfunction, and coexpression of FUS significantly alleviated this motor dysfunction (Figure 2E), indicating that FUS suppresses the neuronal phenotypes of flies expressing G4C2 repeat RNA.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the alleviation of motor dysfunction.

claim: The motor dysfunction caused by the expression of FUS alone was alleviated by coexpression of (G4C2)42.
source: It is notable that the motor dysfunction caused by the expression of FUS alone was also alleviated by coexpression of (G4C2)42 (Figure 2E), indicating that the G4C2 repeat RNA conversely suppresses FUS toxicity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The G4C2 repeat RNA conversely suppresses FUS toxicity.
source: It is notable that the motor dysfunction caused by the expression of FUS alone was also alleviated by coexpression of (G4C2)42 (Figure 2E), indicating that the G4C2 repeat RNA conversely suppresses FUS toxicity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the alleviation of FUS-induced motor dysfunction by G4C2 repeat RNA.

claim: UGGAA repeat RNA reduced the aggregation and toxicity of TDP-43 in SCA31 flies.
source: This result is consistent with our previous observations in SCA31 flies that UGGAA repeat RNA reduced the aggregation and toxicity of TDP-43 (Ishiguro et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: RNA buffers the phase separation of TDP-43 and FUS, resulting in the suppression of their aggregation.
source: Moreover, recent studies demonstrated that RNA buffers the phase separation of TDP-43 and FUS, resulting in the suppression of their aggregation (Maharana et al., 2018; Mann et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Balancing the crosstalk between repeat RNAs and RBPs neutralizes the toxicities of each other.
source: These findings hence suggest that balancing the crosstalk between repeat RNAs and RBPs neutralizes the toxicities of each other.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the mutual suppression of toxicity between repeat RNAs and RBPs.

claim: Coexpression of FUS significantly decreased the number of nuclei containing RNA foci in (G4C2)89 flies.
source: We performed RNA fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) of the salivary glands of fly larvae expressing (G4C2)89 and found that coexpression of FUS significantly decreased the number of nuclei containing RNA foci in (G4C2)89 flies, whereas it was not altered by coexpression of FUS-RRMmut (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The number of nuclei containing RNA foci was not altered by coexpression of FUS-RRMmut.
source: We performed RNA fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) of the salivary glands of fly larvae expressing (G4C2)89 and found that coexpression of FUS significantly decreased the number of nuclei containing RNA foci in (G4C2)89 flies, whereas it was not altered by coexpression of FUS-RRMmut (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The expression levels of G4C2 repeat RNA in (G4C2)89 flies were not altered by coexpression of FUS or FUS-RRMmut.
source: We confirmed that the expression levels of G4C2 repeat RNA in (G4C2)89 flies were not altered by coexpression of FUS or FUS-RRMmut (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: FUS has RNA-chaperoning activity for G4C2 repeat RNA.
source: These results were in good agreement with our previous study on SCA31 showing the suppressive effects of FUS and other RBPs on RNA foci formation of UGGAA repeat RNA through altering RNA structures and preventing aggregation of misfolded repeat RNA as RNA chaperones (Ishiguro et al., 2017), raising the possibility that FUS has RNA-chaperoning activity also for G4C2 repeat RNA.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the similarity to prior findings on UGGAA repeat RNA.

claim: Coexpression of FUS significantly decreased the number of DPR aggregates in (G4C2)89 flies.
source: Immunohistochemistry of the eye imaginal discs of fly larvae expressing (G4C2)89 revealed that coexpression of FUS significantly decreased the number of DPR aggregates in (G4C2)89 flies, whereas coexpression of FUS-RRMmut did not (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: Coexpression of FUS-RRMmut did not decrease the number of DPR aggregates in (G4C2)89 flies.
source: Immunohistochemistry of the eye imaginal discs of fly larvae expressing (G4C2)89 revealed that coexpression of FUS significantly decreased the number of DPR aggregates in (G4C2)89 flies, whereas coexpression of FUS-RRMmut did not (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: Poly(GP) levels were greatly decreased in (G4C2)89 flies upon coexpression of FUS, but not FUS-RRMmut.
source: Quantitative analyses of poly(GP) by immunoassay also demonstrated that poly(GP) levels were greatly decreased in (G4C2)89 flies upon coexpression of FUS, but not FUS-RRMmut (Figure 3F), indicating that FUS suppresses RAN translation from the G4C2 repeat RNA to reduce DPR production.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoassay data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: FUS suppresses RAN translation from the G4C2 repeat RNA to reduce DPR production.
source: Quantitative analyses of poly(GP) by immunoassay also demonstrated that poly(GP) levels were greatly decreased in (G4C2)89 flies upon coexpression of FUS, but not FUS-RRMmut (Figure 3F), indicating that FUS suppresses RAN translation from the G4C2 repeat RNA to reduce DPR production.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the decreased poly(GP) levels upon FUS coexpression.

claim: The 5′ upstream sequence of the G4C2 repeat in the C9orf72 gene affects RAN translation activity.
source: Considering that the 5′ upstream sequence of the G4C2 repeat in the C9orf72 gene is reported to affect RAN translation activity (Green et al., 2017; Tabet et al., 2018), we used flies expressing the G4C2 repeat sequence with the upstream intronic sequence of the C9orf72 gene, namely, LDS-(G4C2)44GR-GFP (Goodman et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The LDS-(G4C2)44GR-GFP construct produces GR-GFP fusion protein by RAN translation.
source: Since this construct has a 3′-green fluorescent protein (GFP) tag in the GR reading frame downstream of the G4C2 repeat sequence, the GR-GFP fusion protein is produced by RAN translation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on the construct design and is supported by reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Coexpression of FUS significantly decreased the expression level of GR-GFP.
source: We confirmed that coexpression of FUS significantly decreased the expression level of GR-GFP, whereas coexpression of FUS-RRMmut had no effect (Figure 3G–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3G–I.

claim: Coexpression of FUS-RRMmut had no effect on the expression level of GR-GFP.
source: We confirmed that coexpression of FUS significantly decreased the expression level of GR-GFP, whereas coexpression of FUS-RRMmut had no effect (Figure 3G–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3G–I.

claim: FUS did not suppress the eye degeneration in DPR-only flies expressing poly(GR).
source: Using DPR-only flies expressing DPRs translated from non-G4C2 RNAs with alternative codons (Mizielinska et al., 2014), we confirmed that FUS did not suppress the eye degeneration in DPR-only flies expressing poly(GR), but rather enhanced their phenotypes, likely due to the additive effects of FUS toxicity (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: FUS enhanced the eye degeneration phenotypes in DPR-only flies expressing poly(GR), likely due to the additive effects of FUS toxicity.
source: Using DPR-only flies expressing DPRs translated from non-G4C2 RNAs with alternative codons (Mizielinska et al., 2014), we confirmed that FUS did not suppress the eye degeneration in DPR-only flies expressing poly(GR), but rather enhanced their phenotypes, likely due to the additive effects of FUS toxicity (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and includes speculative reasoning.

claim: FUS interacts with G4C2 repeat RNA and regulates RAN translation from G4C2 repeat RNA in Drosophila models of C9-ALS/FTD.
source: Together with the finding that FUS decreases not only DPR expression but also RNA foci formation (Figure 3A and B), these results collectively indicate that FUS indeed interacts with G4C2 repeat RNA and regulates RAN translation from G4C2 repeat RNA in Drosophila models of C9-ALS/FTD.
evidence: This claim is a synthesis of multiple experimental findings.

claim: Coexpression of caz suppressed eye degeneration in flies expressing (G4C2)42 or 89.
source: Coexpression of caz as well as FUS suppressed eye degeneration in flies expressing (G4C2)42 or 89 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: caz is a functional homologue of FUS.
source: These data suggest that caz is a functional homologue of FUS.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the similar suppressive effects of caz and FUS.

claim: Knockdown of caz by RNA interference or its hemizygous deletion modestly but significantly enhanced the eye degeneration in (G4C2)89 flies.
source: In contrast, knockdown of caz by RNA interference or its hemizygous deletion modestly but significantly enhanced the eye degeneration in (G4C2)89 flies (Figure 4A–D), indicating that reduced caz expression enhances G4C2 repeat-induced toxicity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A–D.

claim: Reduced caz expression enhances G4C2 repeat-induced toxicity.
source: In contrast, knockdown of caz by RNA interference or its hemizygous deletion modestly but significantly enhanced the eye degeneration in (G4C2)89 flies (Figure 4A–D), indicating that reduced caz expression enhances G4C2 repeat-induced toxicity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the enhanced eye degeneration upon caz reduction.

claim: Knockdown of caz significantly increased the number of nuclei containing RNA foci in (G4C2)89 flies.
source: FISH analysis of the salivary glands revealed that knockdown of caz significantly increased the number of nuclei containing RNA foci in (G4C2)89 flies (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: The expression levels of G4C2 repeat RNA in (G4C2)89 flies were not altered by the knockdown of caz.
source: We also confirmed that the expression levels of G4C2 repeat RNA in (G4C2)89 flies were not altered by the knockdown of caz (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Knockdown of caz significantly increased the number of DPR aggregates in (G4C2)89 flies.
source: Immunohistochemical analysis showed that knockdown of caz significantly increased the number of DPR aggregates in (G4C2)89 flies (Figure 4H and I).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4H and I.

claim: The reduction of caz expression enhances RNA foci formation and DPR aggregation.
source: These results indicate that the reduction of caz expression enhances RNA foci formation and DPR aggregation, compatible with the results of FUS coexpression in flies expressing (G4C2)89 (Figure 3), and that FUS functions as an endogenous regulator of RAN translation.
evidence: This claim is a synthesis of experimental findings on caz knockdown.

claim: FUS functions as an endogenous regulator of RAN translation.
source: These results indicate that the reduction of caz expression enhances RNA foci formation and DPR aggregation, compatible with the results of FUS coexpression in flies expressing (G4C2)89 (Figure 3), and that FUS functions as an endogenous regulator of RAN translation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined results of FUS overexpression and caz knockdown experiments.

claim: FUS regulates RAN translation and suppresses DPR toxicity through modulating the G-quadruplex structure of G4C2 repeat RNA.
source: These results strongly indicate that FUS regulates RAN translation and suppresses DPR toxicity through modulating the G-quadruplex structure of G4C2 repeat RNA.
evidence: This claim is a synthesis of all experimental findings in the study.

claim: The findings shed light on the regulatory mechanisms of RAN translation by G-quadruplex-targeting RBPs.
source: Our findings shed light on the regulatory mechanisms of RAN translation by G-quadruplex-targeting RBPs and propose novel therapeutic strategies for repeat expansion diseases by regulating RAN translation.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The findings propose novel therapeutic strategies for repeat expansion diseases by regulating RAN translation.
source: Our findings shed light on the regulatory mechanisms of RAN translation by G-quadruplex-targeting RBPs and propose novel therapeutic strategies for repeat expansion diseases by regulating RAN translation.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings with implications for therapy.

claim: Expanded G4C2 repeat sequences induce eye degeneration and motor dysfunction accompanied with the formation of RNA foci and the production of three types of DPRs in Drosophila models.
source: We established Drosophila models of C9-ALS/FTD that express pathogenic length 42 or 89 G4C2 repeats [(G4C2)42, or (G4C2)89 flies, respectively] and confirmed that expanded G4C2 repeat sequences induce eye degeneration and motor dysfunction accompanied with the formation of RNA foci and the production of three types of DPRs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), consistent with previous studies (Freibaum et al., 2015; Goodman et al., 2019; Mizielinska et al., 2014; Xu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and is consistent with prior research.

claim: (G4C2)9 flies did not show eye degeneration, motor dysfunction, RNA foci formation, or DPR aggregation.
source: We also established Drosophila expressing normal length 9 G4C2 repeats as a control [(G4C2)9 flies] and found that they did not show eye degeneration, motor dysfunction, RNA foci formation, or DPR aggregation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: In hairpin-forming CAG repeat RNA in SCA8 models, switching the CAG repeats to non-hairpin-forming CAA repeats abolished the RAN translation.
source: In SCA8 models, hairpin-forming CAG repeat RNA was shown to be RAN-translated to produce polyglutamine proteins, but switching the CAG repeats to non-hairpin-forming CAA repeats abolished the RAN translation (Zu et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Small molecules binding to the hairpin structure or the G-quadruplex structure inhibit RAN translation from the G4C2 repeat RNA, resulting in reduced DPR levels.
source: Although the effect of each structure on RAN translation remains largely unknown, small molecules binding to the hairpin structure or the G-quadruplex structure were both reported to inhibit RAN translation from the G4C2 repeat RNA, resulting in reduced DPR levels (Wang et al., 2019; Mori et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Knockdown of DHX36 has been reported to both promote and inhibit RAN translation, possibly due to the different effects on repeat RNA structures depending on the experimental conditions.
source: Knockdown of another RNA helicase, DHX36, has been reported to both promote (Cheng et al., 2019) and inhibit (Liu et al., 2021; Tseng et al., 2021) RAN translation, possibly due to the different effects on repeat RNA structures depending on the experimental conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and includes speculative reasoning about the conflicting results.

claim: Arginine-rich DPRs, such as poly(GR) and poly(PR), interact with LC domain-containing RBPs, including FUS, and alter their liquid–liquid phase separation, resulting in the disruption of the dynamics and functions of membraneless organelles.
source: Recent studies reported that arginine-rich DPRs, such as poly(GR) and poly(PR), interact with LC domain-containing RBPs, including FUS, and alter their liquid–liquid phase separation, resulting in the disruption of the dynamics and functions of membraneless organelles (Kwon et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2016; Lin et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A direct interaction between FUS and DPRs is unlikely to be the mechanism of the suppression of DPR toxicity in C9-ALS/FTD flies.
source: However, we showed that FUS does not suppress eye degeneration in DPR-only flies (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), indicating that a direct interaction between FUS and DPRs is unlikely to be the mechanism of the suppression of DPR toxicity in our C9-ALS/FTD flies.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of suppression in DPR-only flies.

claim: Expansions of repeat sequences cause more than 50 monogenic human diseases.
source: Recent advances in genome sequencing technology unveiled that such expansions of repeat sequences cause more than 50 monogenic human diseases (Malik et al., 2021) and are also associated with psychiatric diseases such as autism (Mitra et al., 2021; Trost et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Expansions of repeat sequences are associated with psychiatric diseases such as autism.
source: Recent advances in genome sequencing technology unveiled that such expansions of repeat sequences cause more than 50 monogenic human diseases (Malik et al., 2021) and are also associated with psychiatric diseases such as autism (Mitra et al., 2021; Trost et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The findings contribute to the elucidation of the repeat-associated pathogenic mechanisms underlying not only C9-ALS/FTD, but also a broader range of neuromuscular and neuropsychiatric diseases.
source: Thus, our findings contribute to the elucidation of the repeat-associated pathogenic mechanisms underlying not only C9-ALS/FTD, but also a broader range of neuromuscular and neuropsychiatric diseases than previously thought, and will advance the development of potential therapies for these diseases.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion about the broader implications of the study.

claim: The findings will advance the development of potential therapies for repeat expansion diseases.
source: Thus, our findings contribute to the elucidation of the repeat-associated pathogenic mechanisms underlying not only C9-ALS/FTD, but also a broader range of neuromuscular and neuropsychiatric diseases than previously thought, and will advance the development of potential therapies for these diseases.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion about the therapeutic implications of the study.
